docs.title: Bash Professional Reference
docs.text:
This reference consolidates the supplied Bash articles into a maintainable bilingual documentation set. It covers command-line fundamentals, pipelines and redirection, text processing, scripting, automation, system administration, DevOps, defensive security, and debugging.

Repeated placeholder material has been removed. Bash behavior that is easy to oversimplify—especially set -e, pipefail, quoting, expansion, and exit status—is checked against the GNU Bash Reference Manual.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
• New to Bash: Learning Path and chapters 1–4
  • Scripting: chapters 7–8
  • SysAdmin/DevOps: chapters 10–12
  • Security and quality: chapters 8, 13, and 14
  • Fast lookup: Cheat Sheet
  • Terminology: Glossary

Run commands deliberately

Test file deletion, permission/ownership changes, service operations, and system-level automation in a controlled environment before production use.

docs.title: 1. Bash Fundamentals and the Shell Model
docs.text:
Bash means Bourne Again Shell. It is both an interactive command shell and a scripting language for Unix-like systems. Bash parses command text, performs expansions, establishes redirections and pipelines, then runs a builtin or external program.

The supplied source articles consistently emphasize three roles: daily Linux interaction, automation, and system administration. Those themes drive this reference.

docs.title: Shell, terminal, and kernel
docs.text:
• A terminal displays text input and output.
  • A shell interprets commands.
  • The kernel manages processes, files, devices, and other system resources.
  • Many commands used from Bash—such as grep, find, tar, ssh, and rsync—are separate programs, not Bash builtins.

docs.title: Short history
docs.text: Bash was developed as part of GNU and became a common shell on Linux systems. It remains installable on macOS, while newer macOS releases use Zsh as the default interactive shell.

docs.title: Check the actual version
docs.text:
bash --version
printf '%s\n' "$BASH_VERSION"

This reference cross-checks Bash-specific semantics against GNU Bash 5.3 documentation, but production scripts should always account for the version actually deployed.

docs.title: Location and navigation
docs.text:
pwd
cd /etc
cd ~
cd -

For operational scripts, explicit and predictable paths are safer than relying on an unknown current working directory.

docs.title: Listing and creating
docs.text:
ls -lah
mkdir -p workspace/logs
touch workspace/logs/app.log

ls -l shows permissions and ownership. -a includes hidden names and -h makes sizes easier to read.

docs.title: Copying and moving
docs.text:
cp file.txt backup.txt
cp -r src/ dst/
mv old_name new_name

Before a bulk change, inspect the selected files with a non-destructive command or the target tool's dry-run mode.

docs.title: Permissions and ownership
docs.text:
chmod u+x deploy.sh
chmod 750 private-dir
chown app:app file.txt

Numeric permissions combine read=4, write=2, execute=1. Apply least privilege.

docs.title: Discover command type and documentation
docs.text:
type cd
help cd
man ls
command -v bash

type reveals whether a name is a builtin, alias, function, or external command.

docs.title: 3. Variables, Expansion, and Quoting
docs.text:
Many Bash failures originate in expansion and unquoted variables.

name="Ali"
printf 'Hello %s\n' "$name"
path="${HOME}/projects"

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• $1, $2: positional arguments
  • $#: argument count
  • "$@": all arguments while preserving argument boundaries
  • $?: previous command status
  • $$: current shell PID

docs.title: Defaults and required values
docs.text:
mode="${1:-status}"
required="${API_URL:?API_URL is required}"

docs.title: Command substitution
docs.text: today="$(date +%F)"

docs.title: Quoting
docs.text: Single quotes keep almost everything literal. Double quotes still allow parameter and command substitution while preventing unwanted word splitting and glob expansion. Variables that may contain spaces or wildcard characters normally belong inside double quotes.

docs.title: Arithmetic
docs.text:
count=4
((count += 1))
printf '%d\n' "$count"

Use a more suitable language or tool for complex numeric or structured-data work.

docs.title: 4. Redirection, Pipelines, and Exit Status
docs.text: Unix-style workflows become powerful when small tools are composed.

docs.title: Standard streams
docs.text:
• stdin: standard input
  • stdout: standard output
  • stderr: standard error
printf '%s\n' "ok" > result.txt
printf '%s\n' "next" >> result.txt
command 2> errors.log
command > output.log 2>&1

docs.title: Pipelines
docs.text:
journalctl -u ssh | grep -i "failed"

A pipeline connects one command's stdout to the next command's stdin.

set -o pipefail
producer | filter | consumer
status=$?

With pipefail, failures in earlier pipeline elements can influence the final status.

docs.title: Exit status
docs.text:
A general convention is zero for success and non-zero for failure or a command-specific result.

if grep -q "READY" app.log; then
  printf '%s\n' "ready"
fi

docs.title: set -e is nuanced
docs.text: set -e does not simply mean "exit after every failing command"; its behavior depends on shell syntax and context. Treat it as an optional aid, not your complete error strategy. Explicitly handle failures at important boundaries.

docs.title: 5. Text Processing and Search
docs.text: The source material gives significant attention to grep, awk, sed, cut, sort, uniq, find, and xargs.

docs.title: grep
docs.text:
grep -in "error" app.log
grep -R "listen" ./config/

docs.title: awk
docs.text:
awk -F: '{print $1}' /etc/passwd
awk '{sum += $2} END {print sum}' data.txt

docs.title: sed
docs.text:
sed 's/error/ERROR/g' app.log
sed '/DEBUG/d' app.log

Take a backup or review a diff before using in-place edits on important files.

docs.title: sort and uniq
docs.text:
cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd | sort
sort events.txt | uniq -c | sort -nr

docs.title: find
docs.text:
find /var/log -type f -name '*.log'
find . -type f -size +100M -print

docs.title: Safer filename handling with xargs
docs.text:
find . -type f -name '*.tmp' -print0 | xargs -0 -r printf '%s\n'

Inspect results with a harmless operation first. Apply destructive changes only after verifying the selection.

docs.title: Inspect processes
docs.text:
ps aux
top

htop provides a richer interactive view when installed.

docs.title: Job control
docs.text:
long_task &
jobs
fg %1
bg %1

Job control is mainly an interactive-shell feature.

docs.title: Signals
docs.text:
kill -TERM "$pid"

Start with a manageable signal such as TERM. KILL prevents cleanup and should be a last resort.

docs.title: Cleanup with trap
docs.text:
tmp="$(mktemp)"
cleanup() {
  rm -f -- "$tmp"
}
trap cleanup EXIT INT TERM

trap is useful for temporary files, locks, and predictable shutdown behavior.

Avoid using fragile text matching such as ps | grep for safety-critical process decisions. Prefer a service manager or a PID/handle you actually own.

docs.title: Shebang
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash

If the deployment policy requires an exact interpreter path, use it explicitly.

docs.title: Conditionals
docs.text:
if [[ "${1:-}" == "start" ]]; then
  printf '%s\n' "starting"
elif [[ "${1:-}" == "stop" ]]; then
  printf '%s\n' "stopping"
else
  printf 'usage: %s {start|stop}\n' "$0" >&2
  exit 2
fi

docs.title: Loops
docs.text:
for file in *.log; do
  [[ -e "$file" ]] || continue
  printf '%s\n' "$file"
done

docs.title: Arrays
docs.text:
servers=(db1 db2 db3)
for server in "${servers[@]}"; do
  printf '%s\n' "$server"
done

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
sum() {
  local a="$1" b="$2"
  printf '%d\n' "$((a + b))"
}

For medium scripts, structure behavior as functions and end with a single main "$@" entry point.

docs.title: 8. Robust Bash Scripting
docs.text:
The supplied sources recommend set -euo pipefail and trap. The intent is useful, but each option has specific semantics.

set -u
set -o pipefail
  • -u: reports expansion of unset variables as an error in many contexts.
  • pipefail: exposes failures from earlier elements of a pipeline.
  • -e: has syntax-dependent exceptions and is not a universal "safe mode."

docs.title: Explicit error handling
docs.text:
if ! cp -- "$src" "$dst"; then
  printf 'copy failed: %s -> %s\n' "$src" "$dst" >&2
  exit 1
fi

docs.title: Temporary files
docs.text:
tmp="$(mktemp)"
trap 'rm -f -- "$tmp"' EXIT

docs.title: User input
docs.text: Keep input as data rather than assembling it into command strings. Avoid eval with untrusted values. Quote arguments and use an allowlist when only a small set of values is valid.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
log() {
  printf '%s %s\n' "$(date -Is)" "$*" >&2
}

Do not log passwords, tokens, cookies, or private keys.

docs.title: 9. Bash Configuration, History, Aliases, and Globbing
Startup files
docs.text: Startup behavior depends on whether Bash is interactive and/or a login shell. Common files include .bash_profile, .profile, and .bashrc. Verify the startup path on the target platform instead of assuming all distributions behave identically.

docs.title: Aliases
docs.text:
alias ll='ls -lah'

Aliases are interactive conveniences, not reliable script-safety controls. Scripts should implement their own safe behavior.

docs.title: History
docs.text:
history
HISTCONTROL=ignoreboth

History can capture secrets. Avoid putting credentials directly on the command line.

docs.title: Globbing
docs.text:
printf '%s\n' *.log

The shell expands filename patterns before executing the command. Handle the no-match case deliberately.

shopt -s nullglob
files=(*.log)

Keep shopt choices explicit inside scripts that depend on them.

docs.title: 10. Networking and Remote Tools
docs.text: Several supplied articles cover tools commonly orchestrated from Bash. They are not Bash builtins, but they are core shell-workflow components.

docs.title: SSH
docs.text:
ssh user@example.test

Use normal host verification and managed keys. Disabling host-key checks trades away an important security control.

docs.title: SCP and rsync
docs.text:
scp report.txt user@example.test:/tmp/
rsync -av --dry-run src/ user@example.test:/srv/app/

Use --dry-run before deletion-capable synchronization.

docs.title: curl
docs.text:
curl -fsS https://example.com/
curl -I https://example.com/

Select timeout and failure flags appropriate for automation.

docs.title: JSON with jq
docs.text: printf '%s\n' '{"ok":true}' | jq -r '.ok'

docs.title: Local sockets on Linux
docs.text:
ss -lnt

Modern Linux environments commonly use ss for socket inspection. This reference does not publish bulk scanning or third-party targeting scripts.

docs.title: Disk use
docs.text:
df -h
du -sh /var/log

docs.title: Services and logs
docs.text:
systemctl status nginx
journalctl -u nginx --since "1 hour ago"

Review dependencies and production impact before restarting a service.

docs.title: Backup example
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -u
set -o pipefail

source_dir="/srv/example"
backup_dir="/srv/backups"
stamp="$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S)"
archive="${backup_dir}/example_${stamp}.tar.gz"

mkdir -p -- "$backup_dir"
tar -czf "$archive" -- "$source_dir"
printf 'backup: %s\n' "$archive"

A backup is not proven until restore is tested.

docs.title: Monitoring boundary
docs.text: Bash is appropriate for small checks and automation glue. Durable production monitoring should use a monitoring/alerting system and a service manager rather than an endlessly growing shell script.

docs.title: 12. Bash in DevOps and CI/CD
docs.text: The source material places Bash in build, test, deployment, Git, Docker, SSH, and file-transfer workflows. CI scripts should be repeatable, observable, and explicit about failure.

docs.title: A small CI wrapper
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -u
set -o pipefail

run_tests() {
  printf '%s\n' "running tests"
  ./scripts/test.sh
}

main() {
  run_tests
}

main "$@"

docs.title: Git checks
docs.text:
git status --short
git diff --check

Automation should not blindly commit and push every workspace change.

docs.title: Containers
docs.text: Use Bash as a thin orchestration layer. Move complex parsing and business logic to tools or languages designed for it.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text:
• Do not store secrets in the repository.
  • Do not echo CI secrets.
  • Treat CI input as data.
  • Retrieve credentials from the platform's secret store.
  • Quote external values and validate constrained inputs.

docs.title: Idempotency
docs.text: CI/CD jobs are easier to recover when rerunning them does not create inconsistent state.

docs.title: 13. Defensive Security with Bash
docs.text: The supplied security-oriented documents emphasize input validation, least privilege, permissions, cautious sudo use, and log analysis.

docs.title: Avoid command injection
docs.text:
Keep data as arguments rather than constructing command strings:

grep -F -- "$needle" "$logfile"

Validate input; use allowlists when the valid domain is small.

docs.title: Permissions and umask
docs.text:
umask 027
install -m 640 /dev/null report.log

docs.title: PATH control
docs.text: Privileged scripts should not trust an uncontrolled PATH. Make the execution environment predictable.

docs.title: Authentication log review
docs.text:
journalctl -u ssh --since "today" | grep -i "failed"

This is for defensive review on systems you administer.

docs.title: Sensitive data
docs.text: Do not put passwords, tokens, private keys, or cookies in shell history, process arguments, or logs.

docs.title: High-impact changes
docs.text: Narrow scope, inspect the selected objects first, keep backup/rollback options, and minimize privileged execution.

docs.title: 14. Debugging, Testing, Portability, and Shell Comparison
Syntax check
docs.text: bash -n script.sh

docs.title: Execution trace
docs.text:
bash -x script.sh

Tracing can expose sensitive values, so use it carefully in production.

docs.title: ShellCheck
docs.text:
ShellCheck provides static analysis for shell scripts:

shellcheck script.sh

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: Keep pure logic in functions with clear input/output. Use temporary directories for filesystem tests. Isolate or mock external operations where practical.

docs.title: Portability
docs.text: A script starting with #!/bin/sh should not silently rely on Bash-only arrays or [[ ... ]]. If Bash is required, declare it.

docs.title: Bash vs. Zsh vs. Fish
docs.text:
• Bash: widely available and well suited to scripting.
  • Zsh: strong interactive customization.
  • Fish: rich interactive UX, but its scripting syntax is not Bash/POSIX shell syntax.

Choose a scripting shell for the deployment environment and portability needs; choose an interactive shell for user experience.

docs.title: Bash Cheat Sheet
docs.text: Goal Example Current directory pwd Detailed listing ls -lah Create nested path mkdir -p path/to/dir Tail a log tail -n 50 app.log Follow a log tail -f app.log Search text grep -n "ERROR" app.log Find files find . -type f -name '*.log' Disk use df -h / du -sh . Processes ps aux Service status systemctl status nginx Service log journalctl -u nginx Archive tar -czf backup.tar.gz dir/ HTTP headers curl -I https://example.com Secure copy scp file user@example.test:/tmp/ Sync rsync -av src/ dst/ Syntax check bash -n script.sh Execution trace bash -x script.sh Static analysis shellcheck script.sh

docs.title: Script skeleton
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -u
set -o pipefail

main() {
  printf '%s\n' "hello"
}

main "$@"

Add set -e only when you understand its exact semantics; it is not a substitute for explicit error handling at critical boundaries.

docs.title: Disclaimer and Usage Scope
docs.text:
This documentation is intended for Bash education, system administration, DevOps automation, and defensive security.

Commands that alter files, ownership, permissions, services, networking, or system data may have permanent effects. Review scope, backups, privileges, and rollback procedures before production execution.

Security examples are for systems you own/administer or controlled lab environments. This repository is not designed to bypass security controls or target third-party systems.

docs.text: فارسی English Meaning پوسته Shell command interpreter and scripting environment پردازه Process running instance of a program جریان ورودی stdin standard input جریان خروجی stdout standard output جریان خطا stderr standard error خط لوله Pipeline connection from one command's output to the next input هدایت Redirection changing the source/destination of I/O متغیر محیطی Environment variable named value inherited through process environments گسترش Expansion shell transformations before command execution الگوی فایل Globbing filename pattern expansion وضعیت خروجی Exit status numeric command result سیگنال Signal OS control notification sent to a process تابع Function reusable shell code block نام مستعار Alias interactive textual shortcut وظیفه زمان‌بندی‌شده Scheduled job task run at a defined time or interval

docs.title: Authoritative technical references
docs.text:
• GNU Bash Reference Manual — primary reference for Bash syntax and semantics.
  • GNU Bash project — official project page.
  • ShellCheck — static analysis for shell scripts.
  • ShellCheck website — online analyzer.
  • POSIX Shell Command Language — portability reference for standard shell language.

docs.title: Project source set
docs.text:
This project consolidates the Word documents supplied by the repository owner, including the full Bash reference, the 2025 academic revision, the corrected revision, and security-focused material. Repeated placeholder/filler sections are deliberately excluded.

When a source example conflicts with Bash semantics, the GNU Bash Reference Manual takes precedence.
